title: Python and Numerical Computing Assessment
description: 12 questions across 2 sections. Allow 35 minutes. Calculations state their units and rounding; review links identify the relevant lessons. The practice pass mark is 80 percent, not an employer certification.

questions.prompt: A 2-by-3 array of float64 values has no object overhead. How many bytes are in its element buffer?
questions.explanation: There are six elements and each float64 uses eight bytes, so the raw element buffer has 48 bytes. Python and array-object overhead is deliberately excluded.

questions.prompt: Vectors [1,2,3] and [4,5,6] have what dot product?
questions.explanation: The dot product is 1*4+2*5+3*6=4+10+18=32. Elementwise multiplication alone gives a vector, not the scalar dot product.

questions.prompt: Why can decimal 0.1 + 0.2 differ from 0.3 in binary floating point?
options: The decimal inputs lack exact finite binary representations
Python deliberately randomises every arithmetic result
All floating-point additions are mathematically undefined
The input is automatically rounded to an integer first
questions.explanation: Finite binary formats approximate many decimal fractions, and subsequent rounding can expose a small difference. This is representation error, not randomisation or undefined arithmetic.

questions.prompt: Which comparison is appropriate for approximate numerical results?
options: Ignoring all differences smaller than one whole unit
An explicitly chosen absolute and relative tolerance
Rounding every intermediate value to one decimal
Exact string equality for every floating-point model
questions.explanation: Choose tolerances from units, scale and numerical requirements. Exact text can be too strict, but arbitrary coarse rounding or a universal one-unit threshold hides genuine errors.

questions.prompt: Apply the trapezoidal rule to y=x on [0,1] with endpoints only. What integral estimate is obtained?
questions.explanation: The trapezoid area is width 1 times average endpoint height (0+1)/2=0.5. This linear integrand makes the endpoint rule exact.

questions.prompt: Why prefer solving A*x=b directly to explicitly computing inverse(A)@b?
questions.modelAnswer: A factorisation-based solve avoids an unnecessary explicit inverse and is typically more efficient and numerically preferable; conditioning still limits accuracy.
questions.explanation: A direct solve avoids constructing a full inverse when only one solution is needed. It does not remove ill-conditioning or guarantee accurate answers for bad input matrices.

questions.prompt: A sample has values [2,4,6]. What is the sample variance using denominator n-1?
questions.explanation: Mean is four and squared deviations sum to eight. Dividing by n-1=2 gives four; denominator n would give the population second central moment instead.

questions.prompt: Ten sequential loop additions each add 0.1. For a stable displayed decimal result, format to one decimal place. What numeric result is displayed?
questions.explanation: An explicit one-decimal format displays 1.0. The underlying binary accumulator may not equal exact decimal one, so display rounding and arithmetic exactness are different.

questions.prompt: Which operation can expose a NumPy view to later owner mutation?
options: Basic slicing that shares the original array storage
Converting every element into an immutable scalar
Serialising values and loading independent storage
An explicit independent copy of the selected elements
questions.explanation: Basic slicing generally returns a view, so changing shared storage can affect both arrays. An explicit copy creates separate storage, though nested object payloads need separate care.

questions.prompt: Which action best supports reproducible numerical experiments?
options: Assume identical seeds imply identical cross-version APIs
Record seeds, versions, data and algorithm settings
Record only a rounded final result in a notebook
Use an unrecorded global random state for every run
questions.explanation: Reproducibility needs the data, environment and method as well as a seed. Library changes, parallelism and algorithm choices can change results even when a seed is reused.

questions.prompt: For A=[[2,0],[0,4]] and b=[6,8], what is the first component of the exact solution x?
questions.explanation: The diagonal system separates into 2*x0=6 and 4*x1=8. Thus x0=3 and x1=2, without forming an inverse explicitly.

questions.prompt: What can go wrong when a data join uses rows published after the prediction timestamp?
questions.modelAnswer: Future or revised information leaks into historical features; use point-in-time availability and an appropriate causal join.
questions.explanation: A row's observation date is not always its publication date. Joining information unavailable at prediction time creates look-ahead even if the merge code runs correctly.
